description_medium: The Associated Press compared statements by Donald Trump and senior officials about the U.S. operation against Iran. Before the February 2026 strikes, officials had described Iran’s nuclear program as obliterated in 2025, then warned of renewed nuclear ambitions. After the attack, they gave several rationales and timelines. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the operation was not a regime-change war, then said the regime had changed. This records shifting public descriptions; it does not show an adopted mission baseline or a resulting loss of accountability.
description_long: AP’s comparison of statements about Iran spans the June 2025 strikes and the U.S.-Israeli operation launched in February 2026. After the earlier strikes, Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the White House described Iran’s nuclear sites or capability as destroyed or obliterated. In the lead-up to the later operation, the administration again described an urgent nuclear threat. AP also collected several explanations for why the new strikes were necessary, some at odds with earlier remarks. At a March 2 Pentagon briefing, Hegseth said the operation was not a regime-change war, adding that “the regime sure did change.” The record supports a comparison of public statements across time and shows that the administration used different descriptions of Iran’s nuclear capability, the purpose of force and the operation’s expected duration. It does not establish one formally defined mission boundary that was later changed, explain why the language shifted, or document a specific oversight consequence. The title’s claim that the messaging blurred mission boundaries therefore goes beyond the comparisons themselves.

description_medium: AP’s March 2 timeline says Trump told reporters at 12:25 p.m. on February 27 that he was unhappy with Iran nuclear talks and had not made a final decision. description_long: The Associated Press reconstructed the hours before Trump ordered Operation Epic Fury. At 12:25 p.m. on February 27, 2026, he said he was unhappy with indirect nuclear negotiations with Iran and told reporters he had not made a final decision. At 3:38 p.m., while aboard Air Force One, he gave the order to launch the operation, according to the timeline presented by Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine. AP reported that Trump asked Republican lawmakers traveling with him to discuss the choice between continuing negotiations and striking; the discussion was described by an unnamed person with direct knowledge. Oman’s foreign minister Badr Albusaidi later said an agreement had been within reach and expressed dismay that the talks had been undermined. These details document a close sequence of public remarks, private discussion and military authorization, alongside a mediator’s view of the talks. They do not prove Trump intentionally used uncertainty to create an escalation option, preserve deniability, or make an off-ramp politically untenable. Those motive claims in the title and prior draft remain unsubstantiated by the timeline.

The administration had asked the court to proceed cautiously after the Supreme Court ruled the previous month that President Donald Trump lacked authority under the emergency-powers law to impose the challenged tariffs. The Federal Circuit sent the matter to the U.S. Court of International Trade, which would determine how refund claims should proceed. AP reported that the government had collected more than $130 billion from the tariffs by mid-December and that the amount potentially subject to refunds could reach $175 billion, according to Penn Wharton Budget Model calculations. The ruling denied a requested delay; it did not decide individual importers’ eligibility, order a particular payment date, or specify how refunds would be administered. The article therefore documents a procedural setback and an unresolved process, not immediate fiscal management or a change in Trump’s messaging.
